title: The empire of Mali
hookLine: the Mali empire grows rich on trade, with Muslim kings and scholars

lines: FRIDAY: NO ROOM LEFT TO PRAY.
A VISITOR AT THE MANSA'S COURT.
cards: Friday, in the capital of a West African king. Get to the mosque late and there's no room left to pray, so people send servants ahead early in the morning with prayer mats, to spread them out and hold a place.
A visitor from Morocco wrote it down: Ibn Battuta again, now at the court of the mansa, the king of Mali. He had complaints.

The welcome gift the king sent him, a little bread, some meat and some yogurt, struck him as far too small, and he said so. But on other things he wrote with open admiration. Today: the empire of Mali.

teach.h: ALONG THE NIGER, NEAR THE GOLD.
teach.b: Mali grew along the Niger River, close to the gold fields of West Africa, where the trade roads from the desert came down to the water.
Its people remember the empire's founder through the epic of Sundiata, a story sung by griots, the keepers of history in song.

teach.h: GRIOTS AND JUDGES AT ONE COURT.
teach.b: Its kings were Muslim, and the court held both worlds at once: Ibn Battuta saw the griots performing before the king, and he saw the judge and the preachers of the mosque. What impressed him?
First, safety: a traveler in Mali, he wrote, had no need to fear robbers on the road. Second, honesty with the dead.

teach.h: SAFE ROADS, GOODS KEPT IN TRUST.
teach.b: When a stranger died in the country, his goods were not seized; they were kept in trust until the rightful heir came to claim them. Third, care for prayer: the crowded Fridays, the clean white clothes.
And fourth, care for the Qur'an, which children were made to learn by heart. That second point echoes a verse.
In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners, and, if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly."
A dead stranger's goods are a hard deposit to return, because nobody is watching. Ibn Battuta noticed.
Gold made Mali rich. What a traveler remembered was whether his bags, and his life, were safe on its roads.

how: In Mali and across West Africa, griots still sing the epic of Sundiata, and Muslims there remember the old empire's mosques and scholars as part of their own history.

s: Ibn Battuta praised everything about Mali
he complained, for one thing, that the king's welcome gift was far too small.
Ibn Battuta wrote that Mali's roads were safe for travelers

games.q: a foreign merchant dies in your town. his goods are valuable, and nobody from his family is here. what do you do?
o: keep them in trust until his rightful heir comes.
send them to the king's treasury.
games.why: Ibn Battuta says that in Mali the goods of a stranger who died were kept in trust until the rightful heir claimed them, and he counted it among the country's virtues.

practice: Picture a map of West Africa: the Sahara at the top, the Atlantic on the left, and the Niger River running inland, away from the sea, before it turns. That bend is where caravans met the boats; trace it slowly as you breathe.
If you pray, remember the people who prayed in the mosques along that river; if not, simply stay with the river.

wordCard.voice: Mansa. The Mande title for the king of Mali, a West African empire on the Niger, rich in gold, with griots, judges, and roads a traveler called safe. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Mali, as Arabic writers spelled the empire's name. Its king was called mansa in the Mande language.

carryVoice: Your line: safe on its roads. Nobody was watching, and the deposit went back anyway. Until tomorrow.
